anchors.label: The performance review (manager/veteran)
anchors.description: A manager 18 months into her role preparing to give feedback to a 14-year veteran about missed deadlines. Both parties have identity stakes that the scripted conversation about deadlines cannot address.
anchors.concreteDetal: Printed feedback document, late-night rewriting, 14-year tenure gap
anchors.friction: The scripted conversation cannot reach the identity layer
anchors.consequence: Conversation ends with verbal agreement and a more damaged relationship
anchors.sourceLocation: Invented fresh for ChapterFlow; thematically supported by diff-conv.txt Ch1 modern example

anchors.label: The sibling care text argument
anchors.description: Two adult children in a 47-message text argument about weekend care logistics for their father with early-stage dementia. Three layers all running; siblings fighting only the logistics layer.
anchors.concreteDetail: 47-message text chain, 4 days long, the word 'logistics' appears 7 times
anchors.friction: Every logistics solution attempt escalates tone
anchors.consequence: Scheduling problem unsolved; relationship cost significant
anchors.sourceLocation: Invented fresh; supported by chapter-map.md Ch1 example guidance

anchors.label: The co-founders vendor dispute
anchors.description: Two co-founders arguing for three weeks about vendor contract renewal. Both have same data. Real conversation is about professional identity and trust.
anchors.concreteDetail: Same spreadsheet passed back and forth with no new data added
anchors.friction: Every meeting ends in the same position it started
anchors.consequence: Three weeks elapsed, partnership damaged, decision still unmade

frameworks.definition: Every difficult conversation contains three simultaneously running conversations: the 'what happened?' conversation (facts/blame/story), the feelings conversation (what each person feels and whether it belongs), and the identity conversation (what this says about who I am).
The conversation about the facts, the story of events, who said what, who meant what, who is right, who is to blame. Most visible layer. Often not the most important.
The conversation about what each person is feeling and whether those feelings belong in the room. Suppressed feelings do not disappear; they distort the other two conversations.
The internal conversation about what the situation says about who the speaker is: Am I competent? Am I a good person? Am I worthy? The quietest of the three and usually the most important.

limits: Naming the three conversations is diagnostic, not prescriptive — Ch1 does not give the reader tools to handle any of the three layers, only to see them
The identity conversation can be clarifying to name to yourself but unpredictable when named aloud to the other person
All three conversations are almost always present simultaneously; a reader who treats them as sequential stages will misapply the framework
unsupportedZones: Identity quake term or AND/BOTH move (Ch6)
Any resolution technique, prescriptive conversational move, or outcome-producing skill
The claim that knowing about the three conversations is sufficient

scenarioAssets.lesson: What we prepare for (the facts conversation) and what the conversation is actually about (the identity conversation) are often different layers
The hidden cost of fighting only the facts conversation while the identity conversation goes unaddressed
When one person names the real layer, the conversation can pivot from logistics to what is actually at stake
The gap between what looks like the hard conversation and what the hard conversation actually is
Recognizing which conversation is making a decision feel impossible
Naming the three layers to yourself changes how you enter the next conversation, even before you have said anything different
